record.paper_title: Open problems on Steiner trees and maximal distance minimizers
record.original_question: For n terminals, among the (2n−4)!/(2^(n−2)(n−2)!) full Steiner topologies, how many can simultaneously realize a shortest Steiner solution?

evidence.quote: Question 2.12. It is known, see [17], that the total number of full Steiner topologies (the underlying abstract graphs) with n terminals is (2n−4)!/(2^(n−2)(n−2)!). How many of them may simultaneously give a shortest solution to the Steiner problem?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the Euclidean Steiner tree problem in the plane: given a finite set of n ≥ 2 points (called terminals) in ℝ², a Steiner tree is a connected planar graph whose vertex set consists of the n terminals together with possibly additional vertices (called Steiner points), with edges drawn as straight-line segments, and whose total Euclidean length is to be minimized. A Steiner topology is called full if every terminal has degree 1 in the tree and every Steiner point has degree 3. The total number of full Steiner topologies on n labeled terminals is

  T(n) = (2n − 4)! / (2^(n−2) (n − 2)!).

For a given configuration of n terminals, several distinct full Steiner topologies may admit geometric realizations that all attain the same minimum total length (a shortest Steiner tree). Determine the maximum, over all configurations of n terminals in the plane, of the number of distinct full Steiner topologies that can simultaneously be realized as a shortest Steiner tree of the configuration. Equivalently, among the T(n) full Steiner topologies, how many can simultaneously give a shortest solution to the Steiner problem?
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a recent collection of open problems on Steiner trees and maximal distance minimizers. A web search did not locate a published resolution giving the maximal number of full Steiner topologies that can simultaneously realize a shortest Euclidean Steiner tree on n terminals; standard references describe the total count of full topologies (Bopp's formula) but not the supremum of simultaneously optimal ones.

status_evidence.title: On the History of the Euclidean Steiner Tree Problem
status_evidence.snippet: The number of full Steiner topologies on n terminals is 1·3·5···(2n−5), originally due to Bopp.
status_evidence.claim: Confirms the count of full Steiner topologies, but does not address how many can be simultaneously optimal.
